source.title: Towards Understanding the Nature of Attention with Low-Rank Sparse Decomposition
source.authors: Zheng-Fu He; Junxuan Wang; Rui Lin; Xu-Yang Ge; Wentao Shu; Qiong Tang; Junping Zhang; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.tranche_reason: The study examines attention superposition in pretrained Transformer models, extending the superposition question from toy feature representations to attention units in language models.
record.gate_note: The authors measure how learned Lorsa attention units are distributed across original MHSA heads. They also report an aggregate estimate in Section 2 that conflicts with the more detailed distribution in Appendix F.2; both are retained. Cited findings from other studies, Lorsa-versus-SAE interpretability scores, and architectural results using Lorsa's imposed 1D OV design are not evidence about the native dimensionality or canonical status of model features.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a methods paper. It builds Lorsa, a sparse replacement for attention layers motivated by an 'attention superposition' hypothesis, and reports Lorsa's interpretability, reconstruction, scaling and case studies. Its one measurement of the phenomenon is how Lorsa's learned attention units spread across MHSA heads in Pythia-160M. That is a related but different construct: attention computations spread across heads, not representational features spread across neurons or recovered from activations by an SAE. It is also defined through the study's own learned units and attribution threshold. So it goes under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V4. The Lorsa-versus-SAE autointerp results compare the study's method with another method. They are not evidence on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right, but it misses the paper's main conclusions. The authors conclude that Lorsa disentangles attention units from attention superposition. It recovers known heads (induction, name mover, successor, attention sink) and finds new ones (arithmetic heads, thematic anchors). It matches SAE interpretability, with 6 wins, 3 losses and 15 ties across 24 comparisons. They report that roughly half of Lorsa heads come from one MHSA head and half are superposed across several. Stated limitations are shared QK circuits, possibly multidimensional QK, dark matter correlated with SAE error, many inactive heads, and cross-layer superposition.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than reproducing the Toy Models of Superposition method, the authors train an overcomplete sparse attention replacement (Lorsa) to predict MHSA outputs, then attribute its learned units to original attention heads.
record.method_sensitivity: The Appendix F.2 attribution threshold defines effective head count as the minimum count whose cumulative contributions exceed 90%.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-160M, about half of Lorsa heads attribute over 90% to one MHSA head, about a quarter to two, and about a quarter to three or more, with no clear layer trend (Appendix F.2, Fig. 11). Section 2 instead states about 25% are multi-head.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention superposition: in pretrained transformers, atomic attention units are distributed across multiple attention heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Reducing Lorsa's QK dimension below the MHSA head dimension (64) sharply raises FVU. The authors suggest QK circuits for attention units may be multidimensional (Sec. 3.1, App. B.1, Fig. 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention units' QK interactions are multidimensional rather than one-dimensional.

record.problems: The reported aggregate estimate in Section 2 (about 25%) conflicts with Appendix F.2, whose detailed categories imply about half of units involve multiple original heads. The distribution is reported as approximate, without uncertainty estimates in the text. The study analyzes Pythia-160M for this attribution result.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant outcome rows omitted. Cited studies' findings and the Lorsa-versus-SAE interpretability results do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity-dependent transition, or feature geometry.
No test of whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity, or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of features spread across neurons, and no SAE feature recovery reported as evidence of superposition. SAEs are used only as comparison and attribution tools.
SAE completeness, stability and canonicality are not tested. The shared Lorsa/SAE dark matter and the majority-inactive heads/features are noted but not framed as tests of canonicality.
Lorsa imposes 1-D OV circuits by design. The study does not test whether the model's superposed features are 1-D.

record.verdict_notes: Attention-head distribution is treated as a different construct from V4's neuron-level or activation-space features, so no verdicts are given. If curators decide attention superposition counts under V4, the Appendix F.2 distribution would be supportive in Pythia-160M. Even then, the Section 2 versus Appendix F.2 inconsistency (25% vs about 50% multi-head) and the method-defined units and 90% threshold should be flagged. Llama-3.1-8B results are qualitative case studies only.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks or sparsity-dependent transition and geometry are tested.
The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The study measures attention units distributed across MHSA heads in Pythia-160M; it does not test SAE recovery of features as a separate finding or feature spreading across neurons.
SAE interpretability is compared with Lorsa, but SAE completeness, stability, and canonical status are not tested.
Lorsa imposes one-dimensional OV circuits, but the study does not establish that the underlying model's superposed units are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Attributed Lorsa attention-unit outputs to original MHSA heads and reported an aggregate proportion of units spread across multiple heads.
rows.measure: Percentage of learned attention units spread across multiple original MHSA heads
rows.note: This aggregate estimate conflicts with the more detailed Appendix F.2 distribution, which implies about half of Lorsa heads have contributions from multiple original heads.
rows.check: Measures attention units (Lorsa heads) spread across MHSA heads, which is not V4's features spread across neurons or SAE-recoverable features. The Section 2 figure ('about 25%') contradicts Appendix F.2, where roughly half of Lorsa heads involve multiple original heads. The value is the authors' own stated number, but it is internally inconsistent.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Counted the minimum number of original heads needed for cumulative contributions to exceed 90%, then reported the distribution of Lorsa heads by that count.
rows.measure: Percentage of Lorsa heads with effective original-head count n
rows.locator: Appendix F.2, Figure 11 and accompanying text
rows.note: For this category, the unit is primarily associated with a single original head rather than distributed across multiple heads.
rows.check: Not a V4 measure. 'absent' is a mislabel: this row is one category share (n=1, about half) of a distribution, not an absent effect. It should be read together with r3-r5 as one distribution.
